CITY OF SOUTH GATE
  REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  MINUTES
  TUESDAY, APRIL 28, 2026

CALL TO ORDER  Joshua Barron, Mayor called a Regular City Council Meeting to order at
  6:41 p.m.

INVOCATION  Tina De La Rosa, Acting Director of Parks & Recreation
PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE  Gabriel Perez, Director of Community Development

ROLL CALL  Yodit Glaze, City Clerk

PRESENT  Mayor Joshua Barron, Vice Mayor Al Rios, Council Member Maria del
  Pilar Avalos, Council Member Gil Hurtado, and Council Member Maria
  Davila; City Treasurer Jose De La Paz, City Manager Rob Houston, City
  Attorney Raúl F. Salinas

PUBLIC HEARINGS

1
PERSONNEL ADMIN  Following the conclusion of the Public Hearing, the City Council
  unanimously approved items A & B by motion of Council Member
  Hurtado and seconded by Council Member Davila:

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Avalos, yes; Council Member Hurtado,
  yes; Council Member Davila, yes; Vice Mayor Rios, yes; Mayor Barron,
  yes.

  a. Conducted a public hearing on the City’s vacancies; and

  b. Received and filed the status update report on vacancies in compliance
  with California Government Code § 3502.3.

  Jon Hamilton, Director of Human Services, gave the presentation.

  Mayor Barron asked if anyone in the audience wished to speak on this
  item.

  Mario Dominguez, a South Gate resident, said the city is willing to fund
  horses but not restore Zoom for city proceedings, and reminded the
  Council about the Public Access and Information Services funds.

  Mayor Barron asked Mr. Dominguez to stay on topic.
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 28, 2026
1
PERSONNEL ADMIN
CONT’D  Mr. Dominguez urged the City Council to fully fund the Information
  Systems Technician position in the Administrative Services Department,
  noting it is essential for operating the call-in feature.

  Jimmy Ozaeta, a South Gate resident, stated that the report shows the city
  hired 45 employees, 23 full-time, and promoted 20 staff during a fiscal
  year projected to have a $9.4 million deficit. However, the report does not
  list hiring dates, job titles, costs, or whether these positions previously
  existed, nor how long any vacancies had remained open. Without this
  information, the reported 52 vacancies lack context and do not convey the
  urgency of the issue. He stated the city cannot cite a fiscal crisis, a hiring
  freeze, and 45 new hires in the same year without providing detailed
  justification. Although the city says the hiring freeze applies to
  non-essential positions, there is no disclosed policy or criteria explaining
  how positions were classified or selected.

  Edgar Pelayo, a South Gate resident, stated that the city is only disclosing
  this information now because the law requires it, and that this level of
  transparency should have occurred earlier.

  Liz Ruiz, a South Gate resident, stated that while the information is
  alarming, she disagrees with the two former colleagues who spoke earlier.
  She recalled that many of these vacancies were discussed during budget
  talks, along with how long they had been open and the challenges of
  maintaining staff morale. She noted that she personally knows staff who
  are leaving and whose positions likely will not be filled. Ms. Ruiz said it is
  hypocritical to raise these concerns now, especially after Council was
  criticized not long ago for giving staff well-deserved raises. She said that
  it is wrong for Council Member Avalos and certain commissioners to pit
  residents against staff, who are part of the community. She hopes everyone
  can work together to support a Utility Users Tax or, if not, propose
  alternative ideas to address the $9 million deficit.

  Having no one else come forward, Mayor Barron closed the audience
  portion.

  Council Member Hurtado thanked staff for the presentation and noted that
  the city has faced a structural deficit for decades. He stated that since
  2012, the city has consistently reduced staffing and held positions vacant
  as part of long-term cost-saving measures. He expressed surprise that the
  two speakers were unaware of this history, emphasizing that the city has
  operated for years without the 100 police officers and 6 code enforcement
  officers it is supposed to have. He added that the 2025 law was intended to
  ensure unions are informed about vacancies, and the city has been working
  closely with them to explain why positions remain unfilled without
  overburdening staff.

  Page 2 of 17
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 28, 2026

1
PERSONNEL ADMIN
CONT’D  Council Member Avalos asked how the vacancy rate impacts overtime
  costs and service delivery.

  Mr. Hamilton stated he could not directly link the vacancy rate to overtime
  or service impacts, noting that some vacancies resulted from program
  reductions.

  Mr. Houston stated that with fewer staff, service levels will decline, and
  programs identified for budget cuts will need to be reduced, although
  some minimum standards must still be maintained.

  Council Member Avalos asked how the frozen positions create hidden
  operational risks or costs.

  Mr. Houston stated that the issue is not just a defined risk but an ongoing
  reality of reduced services, which the community is already experiencing.
  He noted that impacts will intensify after July 1 when final reductions take
  effect.

  Council Member Avalos noted that the Police Department includes two
  CSI-related positions and asked when they were added, stating that these
  positions did not exist when she first joined the Council.

  Mr. Houston stated the CSI positions were budgeted before 2003 but were
  never filled. As budget pressures increased, staff deprioritized hiring for
  those positions despite their continued inclusion in the budget.

  Council Member Avalos stated that although the city budgets for police
  officer positions, it has been difficult to fill them, and the city does not
  want to hire unqualified candidates. She noted that applicants must attend
  the academy, where those not suited for the job are filtered out. She
  expressed disappointment that the Police Department has not reached its
  budgeted staffing levels in the past 10, 15, or even 20 years, stating that
  this long-term gap prevents the city from showing the community that
  their tax dollars are fully supporting a staffed police force.

  Mayor Barron cautioned the Council against suggesting the city failed to
  use tax dollars appropriately.

  Council Member Avalos clarified she did not say that.

  Mayor Barron stated that officers were covering those hours through
  overtime and were actively patrolling during that time.

  Council Member Avalos clarified she was not disputing that officers
  covered shifts through overtime. Her concern is that relying on overtime to
  Page 3 of 17
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 28, 2026

1
PERSONNEL ADMIN
CONT’D  fill budget positions risks officer burnout, which can lead to mistakes. She
  then asked: If the city budgets for 81 officers, how many are currently
  staffed?

  Mr. Houston stated the current number is about 69 to 70 officers.

  Captain Camacho reported a total of 76 officers.

  Mr. Houston stated the department has 76 officers, with some on leave. He
  explained that staffing challenges stem from finding qualified candidates
  and offering competitive pay and benefits. Because the city has limited
  funds and pays below what many cities offer, it struggles to achieve full
  staffing. The city aims to pay at the 50th percentile of the market, based on
  SELA communities, not cities like Pasadena or Manhattan Beach, but
  years of smaller increases have left the city about 10% below that
  benchmark.

  Mr. Hamilton stated that staffing shortages are a statewide issue, as
  agencies across California are struggling to recruit police officers and
  sheriff’s deputies. He attributed this to highly regulated policing standards,
  which make the profession less appealing, and a decline in public
  perception of law enforcement. In the 1990s, the city received about 100
  applications for each position; today it must recruit continuously. The city
  hires candidates and sends them to the academy only after they pass
  background checks, psychological evaluations, and other required
  suitability tests.

  Council Member Avalos asked when the Council would receive the next
  recruitment and retention update.

  Mr. Houston stated that this is an annual exercise. He added that if the
  Council would like a more comprehensive report on a set schedule, staff
  can prepare one; however, he noted that the city is currently focusing on
  many other performance measures.

  Vice Mayor Rios noted the city has long discussed its vacancies and
  continues to face recruitment challenges. He asked how many additional
  hires are expected by the end of the year.

  Mr. Houston stated that if the city starts with 349 positions and eliminates
  32 through layoffs or removal to meet the $9.4 million target, the
  workforce will be reduced to 317 positions, which is the minimum needed
  to maintain services.

   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 28, 2026

2
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING  Following the conclusion of the Public Hearing, the City Council
  unanimously continued until June 9, 2026, City Council meeting by
  motion of Council Member Davila and seconded by Council Member
  Avalos:

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Avalos, yes; Council Member Hurtado,
  yes; Council Member Davila, yes; Vice Mayor Rios, yes; Mayor Barron,
  yes.

  a. Adopting Resolution approving the Fiscal Year 2026-2027 Annual
  Action Plan;

  b. Authorizing the City Manager, or designee, to submit to the U.S.
  Department of Housing and Urban Development the Fiscal Year 2026-
  2027 Annual Action Plan; and

  c. Authorizing the City Manager or his designee to enter into agreements
  with eligible subrecipients in a form acceptable to the City Attorney.

  Gabriel Perez, Director of Community Development, stated that this is a
  routine annual item outlining how the City will allocate Community
  Development Block Grant and HOME funds through the Annual Action
  Plan. Staff recommend continuing the item until June 9, 2026. The
  Housing Manager, who administers the program, is available to answer
  questions or provide a presentation if requested.

  City Attorney Salinas recommended keeping all public hearing comments
  together, noting it would be better to record them at the same time rather
  than splitting them across multiple meetings.

3
MUNICIPAL CODE ADMIN  Following the conclusion of the Public Hearing, the City Council
  unanimously waived the reading in full and introduced Ordinance No.
  2026-04-CC entitled Ordinance amending Title 9 (Buildings) of the South
  Gate Municipal Code by adopting by reference the 2025 California Code
  of Regulations, Title 24 (“2025 Building Standards Code”) and the 2024
  International Association of Plumbing and Mechanic/al Officials Codes by
  motion of Council Member Hurtado and seconded by Council Member
  Avalos.

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Avalos, yes; Council Member Hurtado,
  yes; Council Member Davila, yes; Vice Mayor Rios, yes; Mayor Barron,
  yes.

  Gabriel Perez, Director of Community Development, stated this is a
  routine update required when the state revises its California codes. The

  Page 5 of 17
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 28, 2026

3
MUNICIPAL CODE ADMIN
CONT’D  city must adopt the updates by July 1, 2026. Building Official William
  Campana will provide a brief presentation.

  William Campana, Building Official, stated that Building and Safety is
  responsible for enforcing the California Code of Regulations, which is
  updated and adopted every three years.

  Mayor Barron asked if anyone in the audience wished to speak on this
  item. Seeing no one step forward; Mayor Barron closed the audience
  portion.

  Council Member Hurtado thanked Mr. Campana for the presentation. He
  noted that the state periodically updates safety and energy-efficiency
  codes, and the city must update its municipal code accordingly. While
  these updates are beneficial, they come with costs. He added that
  enforcement is challenging because the city is short-staffed, and residents
  frequently complain about unpermitted work and code violations.

  Council Member Davila questioned the $7,000 budgeted for training and
  asked about the cost of the code book.

  Mr. Campana stated the code books cost $21,000, spread over three years.
  As the city adopts the 2025 codes, he purchased some books last fiscal
  year and will buy the remainder this year. He added that staff participate in
  professional groups that offer training, including some free courses.

  Council Member Davila asked how many staff attend training.

  Mr. Campana replied that the city currently has six staff members.

  Vice Mayor Rios stated that while he understands there are many
  regulations, he wants to know whether the costs relate only to training or if
  the mandates require mechanical upgrades as well. He noted that the state
  often imposes requirements without providing funding and asked if that is
  the case here.

  Mr. Perez replied that this is exactly the case, and that the city must apply
  the updated rules when plan-checking building permits as they come in.

  Council Member Avalos asked how the new requirements might
  disproportionately impact small contractors, homeowners, and
  underserved community members who may not be able to afford the fees.
  She also asked about the fiscal impact on both the community and the city,
  and whether the city will be able to recover those costs.

  Page 6 of 17
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 28, 2026

3
MUNICIPAL CODE ADMIN
CONT’D  Mr. Perez asked Mr. Campana to address the impacts with the greatest
  effect. He noted there are also positive changes, including an extension of
  building permit validity from 180 days to 365 days, allowing applicants
  more time to act without needing to reapply or pay for a new permit.

  Mr. Perez asked Mr. Campana whether the updated building codes include
  stricter standards that may affect contractors.

  Mr. Campana responded that while building requirements have not
  significantly changed, other trades, such as electrical, now face additional
  requirements, and contractors are notified through the State Contractors
  Licensing Board.

  Council Member Avalos asked whether Building and Safety has enough
  staff to inspect permitted work sites, noting many residents still do
  unpermitted work.

  Mr. Campana said the department is managing but falling behind;
  inspections that once took 24 to 48 hours now take three to four days.

  Council Member Avalos stated the city lacks sufficient staff.

  Mr. Campana responded that this is not by choice.

  Mayor Barron asked what would help increase staffing.

  Mr. Campana said the department has updated its fees to align with
  surrounding cities, which may help.

  Mayor Barron asked if that means more revenue.

  Mr. Campana replied yes.

  Jose De La Paz questioned the Board of Appeals section, noting it states
  the five members would be planning commissioners. He pointed out that
  the job and board member descriptions require specific technical
  backgrounds, which planning commissioners typically do not meet.

  Mr. Campana explained that the Board of Appeals was created to review
  the Building Official’s decisions and interpretations, not the building code
  itself. He noted the city has not needed the board in many years. The board
  was originally composed of members with construction expertise, such as
  an engineer, an architect, a licensed contractor, an ADA advocate, and a
  resident, which is why planning commissioners could not serve.

  Page 7 of 17
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 28, 2026

3
MUNICIPAL CODE ADMIN
CONT’D  Mr. De La Paz noted the staff report states the Board of Appeals must
  consist of five planning commissioners.

  Mr. Campana responded that historically the board’s members were
  appointed by the Planning Commission and City Council.

  Mr. De La Paz expressed confusion.

  Mayor Barron asked the City Manager for clarification.

  City Attorney Salinas clarified that Mr. Campana is correct. The Board of
  Appeals has not met in years because there has been no need, and its
  members are not the same individuals who serve on the Planning
  Commission. Serving on the Planning Commission is not a requirement
  for the board, and if the section suggests otherwise, that was not the intent.

PRESENTATION, DISCUSSION, AND RECOMMENDATIONS

4
CITY COUNCIL  The City Council unanimously approved items A and B and directed staff
  to continue the item to the May 12, 2026, City Council meeting for a
  focused discussion on whether to use Microsoft Teams or Zoom by motion
  of Council Member Avalos and seconded by Council Member Hurtado.

  a. Resolution No. 2026-16-CC entitled A Resolution of the City Council
  of the City of South Gate establishing a policy addressing disruptions
  during remote participation at City Council meetings, in compliance
  with Senate Bill 707.

  b. Appropriated of $41,687.50 from the General Fund unassigned fund
  balance to the Information Systems Fund (account 522-305-12-6730)
  to fund the first-year subscription and one-time implementation costs
  of real-time AI-based translation and closed captioning services in
  support of SB 707 compliance.

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Avalos, yes; Council Member Hurtado,
  yes; Council Member Davila, yes; Vice Mayor Rios, yes; Mayor Barron,
  yes.

RECESS  The City Council recessed at 8:38 p.m., and reconvened at 8:45 p.m., with
  all Members of Council present.

  Page 8 of 17
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 28, 2026

5
PARKS  The City Council directed to have Stanford and Willow Elementary
  School students recommend a new park name based on the city's history,
  geography, and neighborhood characteristics, and to return the item on
  June 23, 2026, by motion of Council Member Davila and seconded by
  Council Member Avalos.

  a. Renaming the park located on Southern Avenue between Alameda
  Street and State Street, currently known as Cesar Chavez Park; and

  b. Consider the five (5) names (Southern Avenue Park, South Gate
  Gardens, Farmworker Unity Park, Linear Park, and Unity Park)
  recommended by the Parks and Recreation Commission.

  c. Authorizing the Director of Parks & Recreation to replace park
  identification signs and park benches to reflect the approved name.
6
CITY COUNCIL
APPOINTMENTS  The City Council had a discussion regarding the implementation of a
  Financial Review Committee.

  Guidance was provided for the City Manager to form an Ad Hoc
  Committee, but no vote was taken. The City Council is not establishing
  anything at this time, and the intent is simply to allow flexibility for
  receiving input.

COMMENTS FROM THE
AUDIENCE - NON-AGENDA
ITEMS  Liz Ruiz urged the City Council to consider supporting Assembly Bill
  1627 as part of the City’s legislative platform, stating that the proposed
  legislation would prohibit individuals employed by Immigration and
  Customs Enforcement (ICE) during a specified period from serving in
  teaching or law enforcement positions. The speaker also encouraged the
  City to continue addressing questions related to audits, transparency, and
  public trust.

  Sergeant Peterson of the South Gate Police Department provided
  information regarding the Department’s mounted unit, including its
  formation, operational benefits, and funding structure. Sergeant Peterson
  explained that the unit consists of two officers and their equine partners
  and discussed the mounted unit’s role in crowd management, public safety
  preparedness, and homeless outreach efforts. Sergeant Peterson also
  outlined personal and donated contributions made toward the
  establishment and maintenance of the mounted unit.

  Page 9 of 17
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 28, 2026

COMMENTS FROM THE
AUDIENCE - NON-AGENDA
ITEMS CONT’D  Mario Dominguez commented on expenditures related to the Police
  Department mounted unit and expressed concerns regarding City funding
  priorities, including the use of Zoom for public meetings, holiday parade
  expenditures, and body-worn camera funding. The speaker also
  commented on park naming discussions and requested information
  regarding online meeting viewing.

  Henry Gonzalez, President of the South Gate Rotary Club, announced the
  upcoming Mariachi Youth Festival and distributed event programs to the
  Council. Mr. Gonzalez discussed participating in student groups,
  scholarship and sponsorship efforts, and invited City officials and staff to
  attend the event.

  Jimmy Ozaeta, a South Gate resident, expressed concerns regarding
  comments made about residents on social media and requested an apology
  from the City Manager related to prior statements. Mr. Ozaeta also
  commented on the consultant survey related to the proposed Utility Users
  Tax (UUT), questioning the scope of the survey results and requesting
  additional data and public discussion regarding the consultant’s work.

  David Enriquez, representing Teamsters Local 396, commented on recent
  layoffs affecting approximately 75 Amazon workers and urged the
  community and local businesses to encourage Amazon to restore the
  affected jobs.

  Aiden, a South Gate resident and former Amazon employee, spoke
  regarding the impact of recent layoffs on workers and their families and
  requested community support for affected employees.

  Edgar Pelayo, a South Gate resident, expressed concerns regarding City
  operations, service delivery, and communication with residents. Mr.
  Pelayo commented on the rollout of the proposed Utility Users Tax
  (UUT), use of Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funds, and
  expenditures related to the Police Department mounted unit.

  Ricardo, a South Gate resident, commented on recent Amazon layoffs and
  expressed concern regarding the long-term impacts of large commercial
  operations on the community and local workforce.

  Robin Logan, a South Gate resident, requested that representatives
  involved in conducting the consultant survey appear publicly to explain
  the survey process and findings. Ms. Logan also commented on traffic
  congestion associated with Amazon delivery vehicles near Rio Hondo and
  encouraged the city to discuss related concerns with Amazon
  representatives.

  Page 10 of 17
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 28, 2026

COMMENTS FROM THE
AUDIENCE - NON-AGENDA
ITEMS CONT’D  Francisco Rodriguez expressed concerns regarding the impact of large
  commercial developments on the community and referenced recent
  protests involving Amazon workers and layoffs.

  Jenny Beckinstein, speaking on behalf of Teamsters, commented on the
  working conditions and schedules of Amazon delivery drivers and
  discussed the impact of Amazon facilities on traffic and the community.
  Ms. Beckinstein urged support for affected workers and requested that
  Amazon reinstate laid-off employees.

REPORTS AND COMMENTS
FROM CITY OFFICIALS  Arturo Cervantes, Director of Public Works – nothing to report.

  Tina De La Rosa, Acting Director of Parks & Recreation, mentioned past
  and upcoming community events.

  Gabriel Perez, Director of Community Development, announced a
  community input session on Thursday, April 30th at 5:00 p.m. at the civic
  center to discuss repurposing the courthouse as a community resilience
  center. Funding is available for construction and programming, with
  centers intended for use during emergencies such as extreme heat, floods,
  earthquakes, or fires, and for year-round activities. A flyer includes a QR
  code for a survey, which can be completed by May 18th.

  Luis Frausto, Director of Administrative Services, clarified that the
  funding source referenced by Mr. Perez pertains specifically to grant
  funding rather than city funding. He addressed both todays and the
  previous meeting’s inquiries by stating that audits are conducted by
  independent third parties; the city does not audit itself. Additionally,
  certain audits required by the state or other agencies engage third-party
  CPA firms, such as KPMG, to perform audits of the city.

  Mr. Frausto provided an update regarding challenges experienced with the
  city's water utility payment portal system. The city has signed a contract
  with a vendor to implement a new payment portal, which is anticipated to
  be operational within three to four months. This upgrade will offer
  improved functionality for residents, including convenient access to
  downloadable statements, options for automatic payments, and expanded
  online services that currently require in-person visits to city hall.
  Additional information will be shared as the project approaches its launch
  date.

  Jon Hamilton, Director of Human Resources – nothing to report.

  Sergio Camacho, Police Captain - nothing to report.

  Page 11 of 17
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 28, 2026

REPORTS AND COMMENTS
FROM CITY OFFICIALS
CONT’D  Rob Houston, City Manager, inquired whether City Council has any
  specific input regarding the Amazon matter. The city is currently
  collaborating with Amazon to address their traffic impacts, while several
  unresolved issues from the initial approval process remain under
  discussion. The city continues to evaluate these impacts. However,
  decisions related to Amazon's hiring practices generally fall outside of the
  city's jurisdiction. Should the Council wish to issue a letter of support for
  any group, staff can prepare one at the Council’s direction.

  Mr. Houston clarified that his previous comments were not meant to target
  all social media users. He expressed disappointment toward a few
  individuals who use their platforms to spread false information and attack
  Council members or community members, which he believes harms the
  community and limits potential revenue opportunities needed to maintain
  services. His intention was only to acknowledge this issue, not to single
  out anyone personally. He emphasized that even when disagreeing with
  others, he does not view them as enemies. Moving forward, he hopes
  people will choose a more constructive path for the city's future.

  Council Member Hurtado asked if it's possible to give directions on
  sending a letter even though it's not on the agenda.

  Raúl F. Salinas, City Attorney, noted that the mayor can collaborate with
  the city manager. This approach has precedent; when St. Francis Hospital
  employees addressed the Council, it supported them and sent a letter. The
  item isn't on the agenda due to time constraints.

  Council Member Hurtado mentioned that, as an individual, he would also
  like to collaborate with the city manager on drafting a letter.

  Council Member Avalos plans to draft a letter individually to show
  Amazon that the Council stands united and rejects their treatment of the
  employees who happen to be South Gate residents.

  City Attorney Salinas advised the Council to consider a motion under the
  Brown Act provisions that permit discussion of an item not previously
  included on the agenda. The Council must determine that urgent
  circumstances exist, as suggested by the recent expression of concern
  regarding individuals who are currently unemployed. Bringing this matter
  forward as an urgency item would require approval by at least four-fifths
  of the City Council, based on these findings.

  Council Member Hurtado moved, and Avalos seconded.

  Page 12 of 17
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 28, 2026
REPORTS AND COMMENTS
FROM CITY OFFICIALS
CONT’D  City Attorney Salinas explained that the urgency arose because this matter
  was raised for the first time by individuals informing the Council about the
  layoffs of 75 people and their effect on local residents.

  Mayor Barron asked if anyone in the audience wishes to speak on the
  urgency item.

  Mr. Dominguez commended Council for demonstrating leadership.

  David Enriquez, representing Teamsters Local 396, thanked the City
  Council.

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Avalos, yes; Council Member Hurtado,
  yes; Council Member Davila, yes; Vice Mayor Rios, yes; Mayor Barron,
  yes.

  Council Member Avalos directed staff to draft a support letter from all five
  City Council members, seconded by Council Member Davila.

  Jose De La Paz, City Treasurer, would like to be included in the letter as
  well.

  Council Member Rios explained that the main concern arose when
  Amazon entered the community, prompting questions about their
  intentions for choosing this location. He noted that Amazon planned to
  hire residents of South Gate.

  Council Member Hurtado emphasized earlier today that his father was a
  union member and underscored the importance of consistent union
  support. He noted his presence during the Kaiser strike, as well as the
  UTLA strike, and his active participation alongside the United Health
  Workers Union. Council Member Hurtado also referenced writing letters
  in support of these unions and affirmed his commitment to advocate for
  Amazon employees, stating he will not stand by without taking action.

  Robyn Logan is unsure whether Council is aware, but the Amazon
  employees still have not received their final paychecks. She thinks this
  information should be included in the letter as well.

  Council Member Avalos requested that Mr. Enriquez specify the issues in
  detail so they could be addressed in the letter.

  Mr. Enriquez stated Amazon came in looking for some reason to find a
  breach of contract in their terms of agreement and laid off the 75
  employees that had just recently organized. The employees demanded

  Page 13 of 17
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 28, 2026

REPORTS AND COMMENTS
FROM CITY OFFICIALS
CONT’D  union recognition and were cut in retaliation. The employees have not
  received their final paychecks. The traffic Ms. Logan spoke about, that’s
  just normal traffic that Amazon puts into the city, taking no consideration
  for safety. Amazon is a trillion-dollar company that can afford to fly to
  space. They can afford to take care of their workers. They can afford to
  pay them living wages, healthcare, and union pensions. Amazon is taking
  away work from the postal service, DHL, FedEx, and UPS. Mr. Enriquez
  appreciates City Council’s support.

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Avalos, yes; Council Member Hurtado,
  yes; Council Member Davila, yes; Vice Mayor Rios, yes; Mayor Barron,
  yes.

CONSENT CALENDAR  Agenda Items 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14 were approved by motion of
  Vice Mayor Rios and seconded by Council Member Davila except for
  items 7. Council Member Avalos seconded item 7. Items 7, 8, 9 and 10
  were pulled for separate discussion.

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Avalos, yes; Council Member Hurtado,
  yes (recused from voting on item 11 and abstained on item 14(a)); Council
  Member Davila, yes (recused from voting on item 7 and abstained on item
  14(a)); Vice Mayor Rios, yes; Mayor Barron, yes.

7
ANNUAL REPORT  The City Council approved item A & B during Consent Calendar:

  a. The Tweedy Mile Advisory Board’s Annual Report for Fiscal Year
  2026/27; and

  b. Resolution No. 2026-17-CC entitled Resolution of the City Council of
  the City of South Gate, California, declaring the City’s intention to
  levy and collect assessments for Fiscal Year 2026/27 for the Parking
  and Business Improvement Area (known as the Tweedy Mile Business
  District) Business License and scheduling a Public Hearing for May
  26, 2026.

  Page 14 of 17
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 28, 2026

8
STREETS/SIDEWALKS/
